# Test execution & automation metrics

Execution and automation metrics are mostly measures of the feedback system. They help you judge whether evidence is complete, reliable and timely; they are not substitutes for customer or production outcomes.

```diagram
planned risk / test basis
        ↓
 selected execution scope
        ↓
 run results ──→ pass / fail / blocked
        ↓
 feedback-system health
        ├── stability / flakiness
        ├── coverage denominator
        ├── runtime
        └── diagnosis time
```

## Planned, executed, blocked and pass/fail status

Execution status describes test activity, not product quality. Planned, executed, passed, failed, blocked and not-run counts answer different operational questions and need a stable denominator.

**Practical use:** Show both completion and outcome: executed/planned plus passed/failed/blocked among executed tests. Keep blocked separate because it often indicates environment, data or dependency risk.

> **Caveat:** Do not treat unexecuted tests as passes or failures. A 100% pass rate on 20% of planned scope is not release evidence for the missing 80%.

## Why pass rate is not a standalone quality KPI

Pass rate is the proportion of executed checks that passed under a defined run. It says nothing by itself about whether the tests cover important risks, whether expectations are valid or whether users are harmed elsewhere.

**Practical use:** Use pass rate as a run-health signal together with execution coverage, test relevance, known defects and production/customer evidence.

> **Caveat:** A weak suite can have 100% pass rate every day. A strong deterministic suite may have a low pass rate precisely because it found a real regression.

## Requirement coverage and risk-weighted coverage

Coverage is a relationship between a defined test basis and evidence. Requirement coverage asks which requirements have mapped tests or executed evidence; risk coverage asks whether higher-impact risks receive proportionate evidence.

**Practical use:** State the basis and coverage criterion: mapped, designed, automated, executed or passed are different. For risk-weighted views, keep the underlying risk items visible.

> **Caveat:** A percentage can look complete while the test basis is incomplete. Coverage never proves absence of defects.

## Code coverage and mutation score as specialist signals, not proof

Code coverage measures which structural elements were exercised by tests; mutation testing evaluates whether tests detect deliberately introduced code changes. They answer different questions.

**Practical use:** Use line/branch coverage to find unexercised areas and mutation score to challenge assertion strength where the cost is justified. Inspect surviving mutants rather than optimizing a number blindly.

> **Caveat:** High coverage can coexist with weak assertions, missing scenarios or incorrect requirements. These metrics are evidence about the test suite, not direct proof of product quality.

## Regression completion without a universal percentage target

Regression completion means the agreed regression scope has reached a defined execution state. The scope should reflect change impact and product risk, not a universal “run 100%” rule.

**Practical use:** Report what was selected, why, what remains untested and whether blocked items affect critical risk. A smaller risk-based suite can provide better evidence than a large low-value one.

> **Caveat:** Completion is not readiness. Release decisions also need defect status, residual risk, environment confidence and relevant non-functional evidence.

## Automation health: the governance layer above framework metrics

Automation health describes whether automated feedback is trustworthy, timely and maintainable. It sits above framework-specific implementation metrics and asks whether the suite supports delivery decisions.

**Practical use:** Review flakiness, retry dependence, quarantine backlog, coverage denominators, runtime and diagnosis time together. Cross-link detailed framework engineering to the Test Automation curriculum instead of duplicating it.

> **Caveat:** A suite with thousands of tests is not healthy if teams ignore failures or require repeated reruns to get green.

## Flaky-test rate, retry rate and quarantine backlog/age

A flaky test produces inconsistent results without a relevant change in the system under test. Retry rate shows dependence on reruns; quarantine backlog and age show how much unreliable feedback is being deferred.

**Practical use:** Define whether flakiness is measured per test, per execution or per incident. Track quarantined tests with owner, reason and age so quarantine is temporary containment, not a graveyard.

> **Caveat:** Retries can mask product defects as well as test defects. Preserve first-attempt outcomes and investigate before classifying.

```text
scenario definitions — not universal standards
flaky-rate numerator: tests classified flaky
flaky-rate denominator: tests observed under the agreed classification rule
retry-rate numerator: executions requiring retry
retry-rate denominator: total executions in scope
scope: merge-gate suite
window: rolling 14 days
target: none implied; baseline first, then set a local guardrail if useful
owner: automation maintainers / QA lead
decision: prioritize reliability work or quarantine removal when feedback trust degrades
```

## Automation coverage denominators, in depth

“Automation coverage” has no meaning without a denominator. Possible denominators include eligible regression scenarios, API endpoints, critical journeys, requirements, risk items or supported platform combinations.

**Practical use:** Choose a denominator tied to the decision. If the question is merge-gate feedback, use merge-gate eligible scope; if it is critical business protection, use critical risk/journey scope.

> **Caveat:** Automating low-value cases can raise the percentage while important risk remains manual or uncovered. Show excluded scope and the reason for exclusion.

## Merge-gate runtime and time to diagnose

Pipeline runtime measures feedback latency; time to diagnose measures how long engineers need to understand a failure enough to choose the next action. Both affect developer flow.

**Practical use:** Measure critical-path runtime separately from total parallel compute time. For diagnosis time, define start and end events such as first failure notification to identified cause category.

> **Caveat:** A faster pipeline that drops useful checks can be worse. Pair runtime with coverage/risk and false-failure signals.

## Automation stability vs pass rate

Stability concerns repeatability of the test signal. Pass rate concerns whether expectations were met. A deterministic failing test is stable even though it is red.

**Practical use:** Separate product failures, deterministic test defects, infrastructure failures and flaky outcomes in reporting. This makes remediation ownership clearer.

> **Caveat:** Calling every intermittent failure “flaky” can hide environment incidents or race conditions in the product.

## Summary

- This chapter covers 10 required concepts while keeping tool/formula details tied to a practical decision.
- Definitions, scope, assumptions and caveats matter more than a number or a tool name by itself.
- Claims that depend on a standard or product are grounded in the source registry below.
